result: MYC overexpression (wild-type or T58A mutant) combined with RB1/TP53 suppression in hESC-derived PNECs produces rapidly growing, invasive, and metastatic SCLC-like tumors when injected into the renal capsule, but not when injected subcutaneously. Metastases occurred primarily in the liver and occasionally in the lung, but not in bone, brain, or lymph nodes.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this as the major finding, stating 'the authors provide convincing evidence that RB/TP53 suppression coupled with MYC overexpression in an ES cell-derived model system results in aggressive and metastatic SCLC.' One reviewer notes the limitation that 'subcutaneous tumors don't metastasize, and even with renal capsule models metastases are not common and do not go to important sites (e.g. brain),' but this is acknowledged as a limitation rather than a refutation of the core finding.

result: Previous RP models (RB1/TP53 suppression without MYC) produced only small, benign, slow-growing tumors without invasion or metastasis, establishing the baseline that MYC addition improves upon.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this as established prior work that contextualizes the current study. One reviewer summarizes: 'the resulting RP xenografts lacked important characteristics of SCLC. Unlike SCLC, these tumors proliferated slowly and did not metastasize.' This is treated as accepted background rather than contested.

result: MYC overexpression drives a shift from SCLC-A (ASCL1-high) to SCLC-N (NEUROD1-high) subtype, with RPM tumors expressing NEUROD1 and lacking ASCL1, while RP tumors show the opposite pattern. Single-cell and bulk RNA-seq analyses confirm RPM tumors belong to the SCLC-N subtype.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this finding without challenge. One reviewer notes 'Gene expression analyses revealed that RPM tumor subpopulations expressed NEUROD1, ASCL1 and/or YAP1' and describes the model as showing SCLC-N characteristics. The subtype classification is accepted as a key characterization of the model.

result: Paired primary and metastatic tumors maintain the same SCLC subtype and expression of key markers (NEUROD1, NCAM/CD56, MYC) upon metastatic spread, demonstrating phenotypic stability.
evaluation: Reviewers do not question these findings about metastatic lesion characteristics. The data on paired samples is presented as part of the accepted characterization of the model's behavior, with no concerns raised about the methodology or conclusions.

result: Western blot and RNA-seq analyses confirm that RPM cells express the introduced MYC transgene (not MYCN or MYCL) and have reduced TP53 and RB1 protein levels as designed.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these molecular characterization data without question. These are treated as straightforward validation of the genetic manipulations, with no concerns raised about the western blots or expression analyses shown in the figures.

result: Single-cell RNA-seq reveals that RPM cells have expanded neuroendocrine compartments (2-3 fold increase), increased proliferation (10-11 fold more G2M cells), and distinct gene expression patterns including EMT activation, altered metabolism, and strong MYC-NEUROD1 correlation.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the single-cell RNA-seq findings or their interpretation. These detailed molecular characterizations are accepted as supporting evidence for the model's properties, with no methodological concerns raised about the computational analyses.

result: The authors conclude that full malignant transformation of PNECs requires additional oncogenic changes beyond RB1/TP53 loss, specifically MYC family member overexpression.
evaluation: One reviewer explicitly questions whether MYC might render RB1/TP53 loss dispensable, stating 'If a molecular hallmark of SCLC, such as loss of RB1 or TP53, has become dispensable with the addition of cMYC, this information is critically important' and requests experiments testing MYC with various combinations of the other manipulations. This indicates uncertainty about the specific mechanistic requirements and whether all three alterations are truly necessary.

result: The choice of MYC as the oncogenic driver was based on its frequent overexpression in human SCLC and successful use in mouse models, though the authors acknowledge not all SCLC tumors have high MYC and other MYC family members are also implicated.
evaluation: Reviewers note this as a significant limitation. The editor states 'the impact of the work would have been increased with the inclusion of a broader set of genetic perturbations, such as over-expression of MYCL, to better model major SCLC phenotypes.' Another reviewer mentions the authors declined to test other Myc family members. This indicates the MYC-specific focus is seen as incomplete rather than definitively validated.

result: The authors speculate that metastatic spread may depend on the site of primary tumor growth, suggesting the renal capsule microenvironment may be particularly permissive for metastasis.
evaluation: One reviewer explicitly critiques this limitation, noting 'their data shows that using their model the subcutaneous tumors don't metastasize, and even with renal capsule models metastases are not common and do not go to important sites (e.g. brain).' The reviewer emphasizes this limits how well the model recapitulates widely metastatic human SCLC, indicating the site-dependence is a recognized weakness rather than a resolved mechanistic insight.
